paper_source: Staged bundle in the private papers repository: RFD4-Proteina white paper PDF, https://rfd4-proteina.org/assets/paper/RFD4-Proteina.pdf (169,995 chars of text plus 104 figure images)
show_notes:
**[Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina](https://rfd4-proteina.org/assets/paper/RFD4-Proteina.pdf)**

*White paper — UW Institute for Protein Design & NVIDIA, 2026*

Source: [https://rfd4-proteina.org/assets/paper/RFD4-Proteina.pdf](https://rfd4-proteina.org/assets/paper/RFD4-Proteina.pdf)

**Question:** Can one generative model span proteins, sugars, DNA and RNA in a shared latent space, and does inference-time compute improve real design success?

**Answer:** On the authors' own AF3-judged benchmarks it leads every baseline (10.6% vs 5.9% clustered pass rate for protein binding), and wet-lab results follow across binders, glycans and enzymes — but no evaluation was blinded or independent.

**Three takeaways**

1. One model matches or beats specialist tools for packing, inverse folding and refinement, with AlphaFold3 as judge throughout.
2. Strongest evidence: 89 of 288 phosphotriesterase designs were active, against 0 of 192 from the same lab's previous model.
3. The 158/188 TrkA hit rate is compared across other groups' campaigns, assays and hit definitions, not a controlled test.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hi, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And today we're taking on a big one: 'Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with R-F-D-four Proteina'. It's self-published, by the Institute for Protein Design in Seattle together with Nvidia, and it has not been peer reviewed. Hold onto that for the next ten minutes.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: It's a long one, too. So why this paper? Design models come out most months.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two reasons, both about method. First, the representation. Most design models are built around protein, and everything else — a sugar, a nucleic acid, a modified residue — is bolted on. Here an autoencoder puts every building block into one shared latent space: amino acids, modified ones, sugars, D-N-A, R-N-A. Each becomes an anchor atom plus a learned vector, and the model samples identity and geometry together in that space.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So identity stops being a label you pick and becomes a coordinate you move through.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the idea, and they check it: nucleotides sit next to their counterparts almost every time, modified amino acids next to their parents less than half the time.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. The second number is much weaker than the first.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is, and they report it rather than bury it. They also fine-tune the decoder against a Rosetta energy term, so what comes out is physically plausible.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay, and the second reason?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The word in the title: reasoning. Um — it's doing two jobs. Inside the network they recycle — run the same block over its own output several times — but at every denoising step, rather than once up front. So the model can spend more compute at the stages that matter.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which they market as low, medium and high thinking.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They do. And outside the network there's search: generate many trajectories, kill the ones that look bad, on whatever criterion you like.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right, but a search that kills candidates early only helps if you can tell early. Can you?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the nicest observation in the paper. Across five hundred trajectories they asked when each property becomes predictable from a half-finished design. Interface area settles early, hydrogen bonding in the middle, the folding model's confidence in the interface only at the very end.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Ah — so you prune on area first, then bonding, then confidence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Exactly, each criterion when it becomes informative. On their enzyme example, about three times as many passing designs per hour of compute.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Give me the central claim, then, so we can test it.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That putting all this chemistry in one latent space, and adding compute at inference, buys two things at once — higher design success and higher throughput — and that it shows up in the wet lab, not just in a scoring function.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Two things at once is the part I'd push on. Those usually trade.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The in-silico half first. Four benchmarks: protein binding, small-molecule binding, enzyme active-site scaffolding, D-N-A binding. The metric is a clustered pass rate — distinct passing structures per attempt, where passing means an independent fold prediction agrees with the intended design.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which fold predictor?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: AlphaFold three.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm. So the oracle scoring the designs is the same family of model the field now designs against.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yes. It's self-consistency, not truth, and that's the biggest caveat on this half of the paper. With that said: on protein binding they report about eleven percent passing clusters against roughly six for the next-best method, at something like forty-fold the throughput.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's a wide margin.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is. And the thinking settings do move the number — protein binding goes from under eight percent at the low setting to about eleven at the high one.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And what does the high setting cost?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Throughput drops by more than half. It's buying success rate with compute, which is the honest way to put it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: My problem with the throughput axis is that designs per hour of G-P-U time is an engineering number — it depends on how hard someone optimised the code, and on the hardware.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And one of the two organisations on the author list makes the hardware. They say so, on the first page.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: I'm not implying anything by it. But that axis compares engineering effort as much as it compares models. The pass rate is the part that travels.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed. And every baseline here was run by this group, with their settings and their pass criteria. That's not a question of honesty, it's just what a self-run benchmark is.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is what we saw done properly in episode eighty-one — the blinded antibody challenge, where the organisers held the answers and entrants never saw the assay. Nobody has done that for structure-based design at this scale.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: No. And it matters, because when that blinded test did happen, a non-learned consensus method placed third.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. The wet lab — that's where I want to spend our time.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm-hm. So do I, and it is substantial. Binders first: proteins that bind calmodulin only when it has calcium bound. Twelve of eighteen designs tested did exactly that — tight binding with calcium, nothing detectable without it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's a conformational state, not just a surface. That's hard.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is. The tightest is quoted in the low picomolar range, and — credit where it's due — the authors flag that the estimate sits at the limit of what their instrument resolves. So it's a bound, not a measurement.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Good. That's the sentence I look for and usually don't find.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Then peptide-M-H-C binders, where the hard part is telling the right peptide from near-identical ones presented the same way. They report over a hundred-fold preference for the intended peptide in every case — and two of the off-targets differed by a single residue and by two.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Wait — how were those affinities measured?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeast display with tetramers.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So that's avidity — multiple sites on the reagent, cells covered in binder. The apparent affinity will look better than a one-to-one measurement would.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Which they label as apparent, correctly. The ranking is the useful part there, not the absolute numbers.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Fine. And the headline binder result?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Human Trk-A, the kinase receptor, which has become the field's standard target. They ordered a hundred and eighty-eight designs.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And how many bound?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: A hundred and fifty-eight of them, below a micromolar.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh. That's most of the plate.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is. And they set it beside published campaigns from other groups — the next best of those is eighteen of sixty.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hmm. That's the figure everyone will quote, and it's the weakest comparison in the paper. Different labs, different years, different numbers ordered, different definitions of a hit. That bar chart is not a controlled experiment.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: No. The within-paper comparisons are the ones that bear weight. On selectivity: binders to human Trk-A that avoid the mouse version, which shares most of its sequence across the modelled region — and, separately, designs hitting both species while avoiding the two human relatives. Eighteen of ninety-four came out with that full pattern.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That I like. Designing for a specificity pattern rather than affinity, and measuring against off-targets nominated in advance.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: They also went after intrinsically disordered peptides — no fixed shape to design against — and got binders to most of them, including a couple nobody had designed against before.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: With specificity data?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: An all-by-all panel, five binders against five peptides. Each preferred its own target. One measurement per pair, though.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the non-protein work?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two pieces. Small proteins that shield a sugar so the cell's trimming enzymes can't process it — that's a vaccine-adjuvant trick — and binders that recognise a peptide only when it carries a phosphate, and can tell one phosphorylation site from the one next door.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Sample sizes?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nine glycan designs profiled. It's a plate-scale screen.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right. Encouraging, not established. Let's do the enzymes — that's where I'd expect a model like this to break.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two. So — the first hydrolyses paraoxon, an organophosphate. Their previous model scaffolded six catalytic residues around two metal ions; here they added two more, which demands a more precise active site. Of the designs they ordered, eighty-nine were active.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Out of how many?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two hundred and eighty-eight, and the active ones came from more than half of the scaffold families they tried.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And their previous model, on the same site?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nothing. No active designs at all, out of the hundred and ninety-two they tested.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh — that's a head-to-head. Same lab, same assay, same people pipetting. That's the number I'd build an argument on, not the bar chart.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And the best one is roughly a thousandfold more efficient than their earlier designs. Keep the scale in mind, though — that's a real catalyst, but not a fast one next to the natural enzyme family.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the second enzyme?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: A ligase — it forms an amide bond, and the step they chose is from the synthesis of lenacapavir, the long-acting H-I-V prevention drug. The chemistry is awkward: the catalyst has to push an activated ester toward reaction with a bulky amine rather than letting it hydrolyse in water.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And — did it?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Four designs out of sixty-seven worked. The best converted about seventy-nine percent of the intended amine to product, against under ten percent of the mirror-image one, with no-enzyme controls near background. They also knocked out the catalytic cysteine and lost the activity.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: The knockout control matters — that tells you the designed chemistry is doing the work, not some accidental surface.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah. What's missing is kinetics. These are endpoint measurements — product after sixteen hours — so we know it turns over, not how fast or for how long.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is the whole question for anything industrial. Conversion after a long incubation says the reaction happens, not that it pays.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed. The authors call it a proof of concept, and that is the right label for it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: One more thread — episode ninety, the competition where twelve thousand designed binders went into a pooled cell assay. Every structure-based confidence score there failed to predict which designs would work, and a huge fraction simply never expressed.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Here the denominator is genes ordered, so anything that failed to express counts against them. That's the right denominator.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: It is. But these are still one lab's expression pipeline and one lab's filters. Somebody else running these weights will not get eighty-four percent.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Almost certainly not. Though the weights and code are out under a permissive licence, so that's a testable prediction, not an argument.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is the best thing about this paper, honestly. Let me do takeaways.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Go ahead.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: One: a single model now covers chemistry that used to need a shelf of specialist tools — packing, inverse folding, sugars, nucleic acids — and on the authors' own benchmarks it beats each specialist, with a structure predictor as judge throughout. Two: the strongest evidence is the phosphotriesterase — eighty-nine active designs where their own previous model gave none, same lab, same assay. Three: the eye-catching binder hit rate compares other people's campaigns, and isn't a controlled result.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: What would change your mind?

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Kinetics on the designed ligase. If it turns over fast enough to run a process on, this is a different paper. You?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Someone outside these two organisations reproducing a hit rate with the released weights, on a target the authors didn't pick. Not a benchmark — a campaign.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Agreed. Until then I'd believe the enzyme comparison and the specificity designs, and hold the rankings loosely.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's where I am too. No journal and no D-O-I on this one — it's a white paper from the Institute for Protein Design and Nvidia, posted with the weights and the code. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: See you next time.
